blurb: How machines see: convolutions, vision transformers, CLIP and models that read images and text together.

cards.title: Sliding pattern detectors

steps.p: A convolution slides a small grid of weights, say 3×3, across the image, responding strongly wherever its pattern appears.
Early layers detect edges and colors; deeper layers combine them into textures, parts, and finally whole objects.
The same filter is reused at every position, so a cat detector works anywhere in the frame with far fewer parameters.

cards.aside: CNNs dominated computer vision from 2012 until vision transformers caught up around 2020.

cards.q: The main benefit of sharing a filter's weights across every image position is that…
options: A pattern is detected anywhere using far fewer parameters
It removes the need for training
cards.why: Efficiency and translation awareness. One edge detector applied everywhere beats learning a separate detector for every pixel location.

cards.statement: CNNs assume nearby pixels are more related than distant ones.
cards.why: True. Small local filters build in that assumption, called an inductive bias. It helps CNNs learn from less data but can limit modeling of long-range relationships.

cards.title: AlexNet won the 2012 ImageNet challenge with a 15.3% top-5 error rate — the runner-up had 26.2%.
cards.detail: That gap stunned the computer vision field, which then rapidly abandoned hand-designed features for deep networks.

cards.q: What let 2015's ResNet train networks 152 layers deep?
options: Skip connections that add each block's input to its output
cards.why: Residual connections. They give gradients a direct path through the network. The same idea now sits in every transformer.

cards.statement: ImageNet contains over 14 million labeled images.
cards.why: True. The full dataset has over 14 million images in about 20,000 categories. The famous competition used a 1.2-million-image subset with 1,000 classes.

cards.title: Images as sequences

steps.p: A vision transformer splits an image into square patches, embeds each one, and processes the sequence with attention.
Unlike CNNs, it does not assume locality. Every patch can attend to every other from the first layer.
With little data, CNNs win. With hundreds of millions of images, ViTs match or beat them.

cards.aside: Fewer built-in assumptions means more must be learned from data — but there is more room to learn.

cards.q: Why did early vision transformers need much more training data than CNNs?
options: They lack CNNs' built-in assumptions about locality, so they must learn them
cards.why: Weaker inductive bias. The original ViT only beat strong CNNs after pretraining on a 300-million-image dataset.

cards.statement: A 224×224 image cut into 16×16 patches becomes 196 tokens.
cards.why: True. 224 ÷ 16 = 14 patches per side, and 14 × 14 = 196. Doubling the resolution quadruples the token count.

cards.q: Masked autoencoders (MAE) learn visual features by hiding what fraction of an image's patches and reconstructing them?
cards.why: 75%. Images are so redundant that hiding a little is too easy. Masking most of them forces the model to understand the content.

cards.title: Meta's Segment Anything model was trained on over 1 billion object masks.
cards.detail: Its SA-1B dataset (2023) covers 11 million images. The model can outline almost any object from a single click, even objects it never saw labeled.

cards.statement: Image classifiers can be fooled by pixel changes too small for a human to notice.
cards.why: True — adversarial examples. A famous 2014 demonstration made a network label a panda as a gibbon with imperceptible noise. Robustness remains an open problem.

cards.title: CLIP

steps.p: OpenAI's CLIP (2021) has an image encoder and a text encoder, each producing a vector.
Using 400 million image-caption pairs from the web, it learned to place each image near its own caption and far from others.
To classify, embed prompts like "a photo of a dog" and "a photo of a cat", and choose whichever is closest to the image.

cards.aside: CLIP's text encoder later guided many image generators, including early Stable Diffusion.

options: About 400 million image-text pairs from the internet
cards.why: Web image-caption pairs. Natural-language supervision gave it a far broader vocabulary of concepts than any fixed label set.

cards.statement: CLIP must be retrained to recognize a new category.
cards.why: False. You just write a text prompt for the new category. This "zero-shot" classification was CLIP's headline feature.

cards.title: CLIP labeled an apple as an iPod when someone stuck a paper note reading "iPod" on it.
cards.detail: OpenAI documented these "typographic attacks" in 2021: because CLIP learned to read text in images, written words could override what the object actually was.

cards.q: Many vision-language models feed an image to their language model by…
options: Turning it into a sequence of embedding vectors that the LLM treats like tokens
cards.why: Image tokens. A vision encoder produces patch embeddings, a small projection maps them into the LLM's embedding space, and the LLM attends to them like text.

cards.q: With CLIP, how would you check whether a photo shows a beach or a forest?
options: Compare the image's vector with vectors for "a photo of a beach" and "a photo of a forest"
cards.why: Nearest text prompt. Whichever caption vector has the highest similarity to the image vector is the prediction.

cards.title: One model, many senses

steps.p: Early systems attached a separately trained vision encoder to a finished language model.
Newer models are trained on text, images and audio together from early on, sharing one representation.
Reading charts, screenshots and handwriting; answering about photos; and acting on screens for computer-use agents.

cards.aside: GPT-4o, released in May 2024, was named "o" for omni.

cards.q: Why can sending a large image cost as much as a long text prompt?
options: An image becomes hundreds or thousands of tokens depending on its resolution
cards.why: Patches are tokens. More resolution means more patches, which means more tokens to process and pay for.

cards.statement: Vision-language models are excellent at precisely counting many objects in a cluttered image.
cards.why: False. Counting, exact positions and fine spatial reasoning remain known weaknesses, though they are improving.

cards.q: A model misreads small numbers on a dense chart. The most likely reason is…
options: The image was downscaled, so fine detail was lost before the model saw it
It needs a bigger context window
cards.why: Resolution limits. Many models resize or tile images to a fixed size. Cropping to the relevant region often fixes it.

cards.title: GPT-4o could respond to spoken input in as little as 232 milliseconds.
cards.detail: OpenAI said that is similar to human response times in conversation, because one model handled audio directly rather than chaining speech recognition, an LLM and text-to-speech.

cards.title: Crop before you ask
cards.body: When you share a screenshot with an AI, crop it to what matters. Fewer, larger pixels on the relevant part beat a full screen shrunk down.
cards.challenge: Next time you paste a screenshot into an AI tool, crop it to just the relevant area first.
